About me

From running cloud systems to running AI

I am a cloud and DevOps engineer with about ten years of experience designing, automating, and running enterprise infrastructure on Microsoft Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud. I have built CI/CD pipelines, Kubernetes platforms, and infrastructure-as-code solutions for large financial, retail, and healthcare organizations.

I am now studying artificial intelligence and machine learning at Indiana Wesleyan University. My goal is to work in MLOps and AI infrastructure, where I can combine my experience running reliable, cost-efficient cloud systems with new skills in building, training, and deploying machine learning models.

Newest artifactInfographic + slide deckAIML-501 · November 2026

What It Takes to Train a Large Language Model

Context
A visual explainer of how LLMs such as GPT-4, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA are trained, and what training costs in data, compute, energy, time and people.
Challenge
AI labs rarely publish full training costs, and the estimates that exist use different methods. The information had to be accurate and clear for a non-technical audience.
Solution
I synthesized technical reports, company statements and estimates from Epoch AI and the Stanford AI Index into a three-part visual story, labeling every figure’s source and footnoting my own calculations.
AI infrastructure cost analysisResearch synthesisData visualizationVisual communication
14-slide presentation: download PowerPoint (.pptx) · view as PDF

Key findings

  • Pre-training uses most of the compute, energy and time; Llama 3.1 405B needed 30.8 million GPU-hours.
  • Reported final-run costs range from $5.6M (DeepSeek-V3) to $191M (Gemini Ultra).
  • Frontier training costs have grown about 2.4× per year since 2016.

Experiment reportAIML-501 · TensorFlow Playground

Training Neural Networks: Tuning, Overfitting and Underfitting

Context
Fourteen controlled experiments on how learning rate, neuron count, network depth and regularization change a neural network’s accuracy.
Challenge
Make abstract ideas such as loss, overfitting and underfitting visible and measurable, and compare loss functions the simulator does not let you change.
Solution
I fixed the random seed so runs were comparable, recorded training and test loss for each, and added a short Python experiment comparing squared error with cross-entropy.
Hyperparameter tuningModel evaluationExperiment designPython

Key findings

  • Learning rate mattered most: 0.0001 barely learned, 0.03 converged, and 10 made training unstable.
  • Adding depth and better input features cut spiral-dataset test loss from 0.486 to 0.021.
  • Cross-entropy reached 95% accuracy by epoch 50, compared with 75% for squared error.

Case studyAIML-501 · Training data

ChatGPT’s Training Data: Sources, Biases and Limitations

Context
An evidence-based review of what ChatGPT was trained on and how that data shapes what the model gets right and wrong.
Challenge
OpenAI discloses little about its newest training data, so conclusions had to rest on the best-documented model and published research.
Solution
I analyzed the GPT-3 training mixture, documented language, demographic and labeler biases, and explained limitations such as knowledge cutoffs and test-set contamination.
Data quality analysisAI ethics & biasTechnical writing
93%

of the words in GPT-3’s training data were English, one reason the model performs best for English-speaking users (Brown et al., 2020).

Key findings

  • GPT-3 was trained mostly on filtered Common Crawl web text (60% of the mix), plus Reddit-linked pages, books and Wikipedia.
  • The data carries language, demographic and stereotype biases, and fine-tuning adds the preferences of a small group of labelers.
  • Fixed knowledge cutoffs and no built-in fact-checking mean outputs should be verified before they are relied on.
